amendments.rule: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written*, `הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא` → *The priest that offereth* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. **But read where the ASV has put the attributive before reaching for that sentence.** Where it renders the attributive prenominally instead, no relative stands before the attributive's own word and rule 47 governs the count: the phrase's single *the* is the first article's and the agreement article is `unrepresented`, as `הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ` → *the anointed priest* is. **A demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner the ASV writes in the article's place goes the same way, whatever the article stands on.** Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase but a *this*, *that*, *these*, *those*, a possessive *his*, *her*, *thy*, *thine*, or a quantifier such as *any* or *every*, standing where the phrase's *the* would stand — `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness*, `הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thine elder*, `הַבֶּגֶד` → *any garment* — that word is what the ASV has written for the article: the article takes it and heads on it, and it is neither `added` nor a reason to mark the article `unrepresented`. A quantifying determiner is read on exactly the terms of the others and is not left to the noun under rule 15: that rule gives a supplied *any* to the nominal expression only where no determiner morpheme stands before the word it determines, and an article standing on that word is such a morpheme. **Read that as no *the* standing before the article's own word, not as no *the* anywhere in the phrase.** Where the article sits on the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain and the ASV writes a *the* before the construct and a demonstrative or possessive before the rectum's own word, rule 29's arthrous case governs the count: nothing is fronted, the article takes the determiner standing before its own word, and the construct takes the supplied *the*. `יְמֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה` → *the days of* ***their*** *feasting* gives *their* to the article and *the days* to the construct, exactly as `שְׂדֵה הָעִיר` → *the fields of the city* gives the second *the* to the article there. Do not mark such an article `unrepresented` and the determiner `added` under rule 18's closing sentence: that sentence governs a supplied possessive with no determiner morpheme standing before the word it determines, and here one does. **But only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner.** A pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase is rendered by a possessive of its own under rule 18, a `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what an *any* or an *every* renders under rule 15, an `אֶחָד` standing in the phrase is itself what a distributive *each* or *every* renders, and a demonstrative pronoun standing in the phrase is itself what a written *this*, *that*, *these* or *those* renders; where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase that morpheme takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second; so too `אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר` → *their eldest brother's*, where the suffix takes *their* and the article has nothing, and `הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *that place*, where `הוּא` takes the written *that* while the noun's article and the agreement article beside it are both `unrepresented` under rule 47. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. **The `אֶחָד` case is counted on exactly those terms, and it turns on the one word the ASV wrote rather than on where that word stands.** A distributive determiner stands precisely where the phrase's *the* would stand, so the preceding sentences alone would hand it to the article; the numeral takes it because the numeral is itself what the word says. Where the ASV writes one such determiner, it is the numeral's and every article in the phrase — the noun's own and the agreement article on the numeral alike — is `unrepresented`: `לַפָּר הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***each*** *bullock* and `לַכֶּבֶשׂ הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***every*** *lamb*. Where it instead writes a *the* before the noun and an *one* for the numeral, two determiners are written and each morpheme takes the one standing before its own word: `לָאַיִל הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***the one*** *ram* gives *the* to the noun's article and *one* to the numeral, the agreement article still `unrepresented` under rule 47. One verse may write both shapes, and NUM.28.12 and NUM.28.28 do. The corpus aligns `אֶחָד` to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so a numeral standing in the phrase is a morpheme that licenses such a determiner; the article's own units of *every* are the case this sentence excludes, where no such numeral stands. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentence has left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction.
amendments.why: Rule 41's limit list named `כֹּל`, a pronominal suffix and a demonstrative pronoun, but no numeral, while its main determiner sentence gives a quantifying determiner to the article whenever that word stands where the phrase's *the* would stand. NUM.28 writes `לַ<noun> הָאֶחָד` fourteen times, and the ASV renders it *for each bullock*, *for every lamb* and *for the one ram* — so the rule as written would have handed *each* and *every* to the article and left `אֶחָד` `unrepresented`, and a chapter reading rule 41 literally would have split from one reading it half that way. The corpus carried the correction rather than this chapter alone: `אֶחָד` is aligned directly to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so the numeral is a morpheme that licenses the determiner in the sense the limit already uses for `כֹּל`. The amendment adds `אֶחָד` to that list and states the count for the *the one X* shape, where two determiners are written and each morpheme takes its own; nothing else in the rule is altered.

conventions: Distributive repetition of the form `X בְּXוֹ` — `שַׁבַּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ` (v.10), `חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ` (v.14) — gives the ASV's single *every* to the `בְּ`, which is what makes the phrase distributive, while the repeated noun and its resumptive suffix are `unrepresented` under rule 22 and the first occurrence keeps its own noun and its relational *of*. Giving *every* instead to the first noun as a supplied determiner under rule 15 was the competing reading; it is not promoted to a rule because no corpus evidence for the construction was consulted, so a later chapter with that evidence may settle it differently.

In `לַ<noun> הָאֶחָד`, count the determiners the ASV wrote. Where it writes one distributive determiner, `אֶחָד` takes it and both articles in the phrase — the noun's own and the agreement article on the numeral — are `unrepresented`: *for each bullock* (vv.12, 28), *unto/for every lamb* (vv.13, 21, 29). Where it writes *the one X*, two determiners are written and each morpheme takes its own: the noun's article takes *the* and `אֶחָד` takes *one*, the agreement article still `unrepresented` (vv.7, 12, 14, 28). Promoted as an amendment to rule 41.

`לַ[הַ]יּוֹם` is divided two ways in this chapter, on the English and not on the Hebrew. At v.3 the ASV writes *day by day*, so the preposition takes *by*, the noun takes both occurrences of *day* in one discontinuous unit under rule 25, and the assimilated article is `unrepresented`. At v.24 it writes the single word *daily*, so all three morphemes share one unit headed on the noun under rule 30. Do not read the second as licence to fuse the first, or the first as licence to split the second.

The chapter's two `בְּנֵי` constructs are not treated alike, because the ASV spends a different number of words on them. `בְּנֵי בָקָר` → *young* is one fused unit headed on `בֵּן`, with `בָּקָר` inside it rather than `unrepresented` beside it (vv.11, 19, 27). `בְּנֵי שָׁנָה` → *old* leaves `שָׁנָה` its own *a year*, so the two morphemes are split under rule 2 (vv.3, 9, 11, 19, 27). Likewise the supplied specifier *he* joins the noun's unit in `כְּבָשִׂים` → *he lambs* and in `שְׂעִיר` → *he goat* (v.22), but where `עִזִּים` is written it is that morpheme's *he* and the construct keeps only *goat* (vv.15, 30).

In the verbless offering formula the ASV's whole supplied subject-and-copula goes to the predicate `עֹלַת`, whichever dummy it chooses: *It is a continual burnt offering* (v.6) and *this is the burnt offering of every sabbath* (v.10) are read alike, and the supplied demonstrative is not `added`. Where `זֹאת` is written the pronoun takes *this* alone and only the copula joins the predicate (v.14). Reading v.10's *this* as `added` would split one construction on the ASV's choice of dummy word.

Supplied generics and ASV italics that expand one substantive join that substantive's unit and never head it: *part*/*parts* on `עִשָּׂרוֹן` and on the ordinals `רְבִיעִת`, `שְׁלִישִׁת`, `עֲשִׂירִית`; the italic *of an ephah* on `עִשָּׂרוֹן` where the ASV writes it (vv.9, 12) and not where it does not (vv.12b, 13, 20, 21, 28, 29); the italic *feast of* on `שָׁבֻעֹתֵיכֶם` (v.26). The chapter's only `added` units are the supplied object pronouns *it* (v.8) and *them* (v.31), where no object morpheme stands in the clause.

Recurring head choices for the offering vocabulary, held constant across all 31 verses: `עֹלָה`→*burnt*, `מִנְחָה`→*meal*, `נֶסֶךְ`→*drink*, `אִשֶּׁה`→*fire*, `חַטָּאת`→*sin*, `סֹלֶת`→*fine*, `שֵׁכָר`→*strong*, `עִשָּׂרוֹן`→*tenth*, `רֵיחַ`→*savor*, `קֹדֶשׁ`→*holy*, `תָּמִים`→*blemish*, `מִלְּבַד`→*besides* on `בַד`. `מוֹעֵד` → *due season* heads on *season* instead, and the contrast with `סֹלֶת` → *fine flour* is deliberate: rule 31's tie-break turns on whether the ASV writes the English noun alone for that Hebrew word elsewhere, which it does for *season* and does not for *flour*.

The corpus aligns `אֶחָד` to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so a numeral standing in the phrase is a morpheme that licenses such a determiner; the article's own units of *every* are the case this sentence excludes, where no such numeral stands. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentence has left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction.
amended.why: Rule 41's limit list named `כֹּל`, a pronominal suffix and a demonstrative pronoun, but no numeral, while its main determiner sentence gives a quantifying determiner to the article whenever that word stands where the phrase's *the* would stand. NUM.28 writes `לַ<noun> הָאֶחָד` fourteen times, and the ASV renders it *for each bullock*, *for every lamb* and *for the one ram* — so the rule as written would have handed *each* and *every* to the article and left `אֶחָד` `unrepresented`, and a chapter reading rule 41 literally would have split from one reading it half that way. The corpus carried the correction rather than this chapter alone: `אֶחָד` is aligned directly to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so the numeral is a morpheme that licenses the determiner in the sense the limit already uses for `כֹּל`. The amendment adds `אֶחָד` to that list and states the count for the *the one X* shape, where two determiners are written and each morpheme takes its own; nothing else in the rule is altered.

report: Read all 37 candidate lemma groups and then the full verse dump, since the table is keyed by source lemma and cannot see `added` units or a supplied word folded one way in one verse and another way elsewhere. No genuine cross-verse split found; patches array is empty.

The two identical-Hebrew pairs that received different treatments are ASV differences the source licenses. `לַ[הַ]יּוֹם` is split as *by* + *day ... day* with the article unrepresented at v.3, and fused as *daily* at v.24; rule 30's one-rendering condition is what separates them, and both verses name the competing reading. `לַ[הַ]כֶּבֶשׂ הָאֶחָד` is *for the one lamb* at v.7 and *for every lamb* at vv.13, 21, 29; the chapter's rule is uniform — a written *the* goes to the noun's article with *one* on the numeral, a written *each*/*every* goes to the numeral with both articles unrepresented. vv.12 and 28 write both shapes in one verse and divide them that way.

Distributive repetition is uniform: `שַׁבַּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ` (v.10) and `חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ` (v.14) both give the single *every* to the `בְּ` and mark the repeated noun and its suffix `unrepresented` under rule 22; `עִשָּׂרוֹן עִשָּׂרוֹן` (vv.13, 21, 29) marks the second occurrence `unrepresented` with the distributive carried by `הָאֶחָד`. In every case the word goes to the one morpheme in the construction that is not itself the repetition.

Supplied English is folded consistently throughout: supplied *the*, *a*, *of*, *for*, the copulas, the generic *part(s)*, the italic *of an ephah* (vv.9, 12) and the italic *feast of* (v.26) all join the unit of the morpheme that licenses them. The chapter's only two `added` units are the supplied object pronouns *it* (v.8) and *them* (v.31), in clauses with no object morpheme — rule 44's express case, and they agree with each other.

All 26 BSB disagreements are documented convention differences, not errors: the `לֵאמֹר` lamed at v.1 (rule 27), 17 articles the ASV writes no *the* for (rule 29), the object markers at vv.4, 8, 23 (rule 16), the `לָכֶם` of the possessive recasting at vv.25-26 (rules 40, 43), and the distributive repetitions at vv.13, 14, 21, 29 (rule 22), where BSB attaches each occurrence to its own phrase. Nothing here should move.

Two edges I looked at hardest and left standing, both already hedged in their verse notes: v.5's supplied *of* before *beaten oil*, given to `שֶׁמֶן` although that noun already carries a `בְּ` rendered *with*, so rule 33's `no preposition on it` condition is strictly unmet and `added` is the live alternative; and `בִּכּוּרִים` → *first fruits* headed on *first*, where rule 31's subtraction ties. Three large-source-unit flags (vv.23, 24, 31) are all correct: `מִלְּבַד` → *besides* twice, headed on `בַד`, and `לַ[הַ]יּוֹם` → *daily*. Each meets rule 30's one-rendering condition.
